extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in California legal history and freedom-of-expression law
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the legal standards, elements, penalties, and historical/judicial context of the California Criminal Syndicalism Act (1919). Useful for historians, legal researchers, or students studying repression of political movements and free‑speech jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prohibition: criminalization of syndicalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The California Criminal Syndicalism Act (Stats. 1919, c. 188, p. 281; codified at California Penal Code §§ 11400 et seq.) was a law of California in 1919 criminalizing syndicalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states the Act 'criminaliz[ed] syndicalism' and identifies its statutory citation and year of enactment (enacted April 30, 1919). Use this as the baseline legal prohibition described by the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements for conviction: membership or advocacy as sufficient grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: "any person who was a member of any organization that advocated criminal syndicalism was guilty of a felony"; "Simple advocacy of a certain belief or membership in a group that advocated syndicalism was enough to secure a conviction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act did not require commission of an overt criminal act; mere membership in or advocacy by an organization could satisfy the statute's elements. This is emphasized as the Act's significant and controversial feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: No overt act required
rubrics_metrics.description: A person did not have to commit any overt act; simple advocacy or membership alone could result in conviction under the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This feature is repeatedly noted as legally and historically significant (i.e., the law made certain beliefs illegal). It explains why the statute was constitutionally controversial and led to major court challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations were punishable by felony conviction and up to 14 years in state prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article quotes: convicted persons were 'punishable by up to 14 years in the state prison.' It also documents actual sentences imposed in prosecutions (e.g., sentences ranging up to 42 years in one case, deportation in others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enactment and repeal dates / statutory lifecycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Enacted April 30, 1919; repealed in 1991 (repealed by California Stats. 1991, c. 186 (A.B. 436)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives both the original enactment date and the repeal statute. Use these dates to delimit the statute's period of effect (1919–1991).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial history: Whitney v. California and Brandenburg v. Ohio
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act was upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in Whitney v. California (1927) but Whitney was explicitly overturned by Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), effectively declaring the Act unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two Supreme Court decisions mark the statute's constitutional trajectory: initial validation (Whitney) and later repudiation (Brandenburg). The article highlights Whitney as a best-known conviction leading to the 1927 decision, and Brandenburg as the decision that undermined statutes of this kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical context: First Red Scare and labor unrest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act must be viewed in the context of the First Red Scare and the turbulent labor history of the United States in the early 20th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article situates the statute within broader social and political forces (anti-radical sentiment, labor conflict). Use this to interpret the statute as part of a wider pattern of repression during that era.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-level diffusion: adoption by other states
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1910 to 1920, 20 states enacted laws criminalizing syndicalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows the Act was part of a nationwide trend; comparisons to other states' laws are relevant when assessing the statute's significance and commonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convictions and prosecutions data (examples and outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists notable prosecutions and statistics: Charlotte Anita Whitney's conviction (1920); Imperial Valley/AWIL raids in April 1930 with 531 indictments statewide 1919–1924 per McWilliams (264 tried, 164 convicted, 128 sentenced to San Quentin for 1–14 years); some reversals (e.g., Frank Spector reversed in 1931); many paroled by 1933.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these prosecution examples and summary statistics as empirical evidence of how the statute was enforced and its practical effects (e.g., long sentences, deportations, later reversals and paroles). The AWIL/Imperial Valley case provides a concrete example of mass enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act was codified at California Penal Code §§ 11400 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory citation is provided for legal lookup and cross-reference; include it when citing the law or locating its text in historical codes.
